title: Biden v. Missouri (2022)
shortTitle: Biden v. Missouri (2022) — brief comparison note
summary: The Secretary of Health and Human Services may require staff at Medicare and Medicaid facilities to be vaccinated against COVID-19 because the statutes let him impose conditions necessary for patient health and safety.
notes:
Key line: "After all, ensuring that providers take steps to avoid transmitting a dangerous virus to their patients is consistent with the fundamental principle of the medical profession: first, do no harm." Per curiam opinion.

Citation: 595 U.S. 87 (2022).

sections.Parties: Applicants were President Biden, Secretary of Health and Human Services Xavier Becerra and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, which issued the vaccination rule. Respondents were two groups of states, one led by Missouri and one led by Louisiana, which had obtained injunctions against the rule in district courts. The states argued that the Secretary lacked statutory authority and had skipped required notice and comment. The Government argued that the rule fell within the Secretary's long-standing power to set conditions of participation protecting patients.
sections.Material Facts: Medicare and Medicaid provide health coverage for elderly, disabled and low-income Americans, and the Secretary has general authority under 42 U.S.C. 1302(a) to adopt regulations necessary for efficient administration and specific authority under provisions such as 42 U.S.C. 1395x(e)(9) to impose requirements he finds necessary in the interest of the health and safety of individuals furnished services. Facilities have long had to maintain infection prevention and control programs. On November 5, 2021, the Secretary issued an interim final rule, 86 Fed. Reg. 61555, requiring participating facilities to ensure their staff are vaccinated against COVID-19, with medical and religious exemptions and an exception for full-time teleworkers. The Secretary found that 35 percent or more of staff remained unvaccinated at many facilities and that unvaccinated workers spread the virus to vulnerable patients. He found good cause to skip notice and comment because of the coming winter surge.
sections.Procedural History: Missouri and other states sued in the Eastern District of Missouri, and Louisiana and other states sued in the Western District of Louisiana. Both district courts issued preliminary injunctions in late November 2021, the Louisiana injunction reaching every state not covered by the Missouri order. The Eighth and Fifth Circuits declined to stay the injunctions. The Government applied to the Supreme Court for stays. The Court heard argument on January 7, 2022, together with the OSHA case, and on January 13, 2022 granted the applications and stayed both injunctions.
sections.Issue: The Medicare and Medicaid statutes let the Secretary of Health and Human Services set conditions of participation that he finds necessary in the interest of the health and safety of patients, and he invoked that authority to require vaccination of staff at participating facilities through an interim final rule issued without notice and comment. Two district courts enjoined the rule. Was the Government likely to succeed in showing that the Secretary had statutory authority to condition participation on staff vaccination and that he had good cause to skip notice and comment, so that the injunctions should be stayed?
sections.Holding: Yes. The Secretary's authority to impose conditions he finds necessary in the interest of the health and safety of patients plainly covers a requirement that facility staff be vaccinated against a dangerous virus, and the rule fits within the longstanding practice of regulating infection control. The Secretary also had good cause to forgo notice and comment given the pandemic. The injunctions were stayed.
sections.Reasoning: The per curiam opinion stressed that ensuring facilities protect patients is perhaps the most basic function of the Secretary's programs, and the statutes expressly authorize conditions the Secretary finds necessary for patient health and safety. The Secretary determined that a vaccine requirement would substantially reduce transmission from healthcare workers to patients, a finding within his expertise. The Court noted that Congress had long accepted detailed conditions of participation, including requirements that staff be trained in infection control and that hospitals maintain infection prevention programs, and that states routinely require healthcare workers to be vaccinated against diseases such as hepatitis B and influenza. Unlike the OSHA mandate, this rule addressed a hazard specific to the regulated setting: patients in hospitals and nursing homes are especially vulnerable, and the workers regulated are those who care for them. The Court rejected the argument that the rule fell under a provision barring federal control over the selection and tenure of medical personnel, reading that provision as addressing day-to-day management rather than participation conditions. It also found that the Secretary reasonably concluded that delay would cost lives, satisfying the good-cause exception, and that the two-month gap after the President's announcement did not undermine that finding.

topics.lrs-i-major-questions: The short note supplies a contrasting emergency outcome under a healthcare-specific program; the full rationale is not included.

learning.separateOpinions: The vote was 5 to 4. Justice Thomas dissented, joined by Justices Alito, Gorsuch and Barrett, arguing that the scattered statutory provisions the Government cited addressed administrative matters and did not clearly authorize a mandate covering 10 million workers, so the states were likely to prevail. Justice Alito also dissented, joined by Justices Thomas, Gorsuch and Barrett, faulting the Secretary for skipping notice and comment and the Court for allowing a rule of this magnitude to take effect on an emergency docket without full review.
